topic.timeline_arc: June 2025 marked proactive local actions and early warnings as cities in India, Mexico, and Pakistan prepared for intensifying urban floods, with research highlighting low‑impact development tools. July’s deadly monsoon floods across South Asia exposed crumbling drainage systems and triggered calls for trillion‑dollar upgrades to build resilient, low‑carbon infrastructure. By September, governments responded with large‑scale plans such as Delhi’s 30‑year Drainage Master Plan, while the Caribbean and U.S. also faced storm‑driven flooding. Late‑year events, especially November’s record downpours, shifted the discourse toward nature‑based mitigation and the deployment of lidar‑based detection and AI‑driven flood intelligence. Entering 2026, the focus turned to advanced technologies and ambitious financing, from AI‑enhanced drainage control in the Dominican Republic to massive drainage master plans and climate‑tech sensor networks, while record rains continued to test urban resilience.
turning_points: Proactive local measures, early forecasts, and research on low‑impact development set a baseline for flood preparedness.

text.summary: Coverage of urban flooding totals 667 articles between 2024-06 and 2026-05, and its direction is falling, with the last third of the window at 0.72 of the first third. Coverage peaked in 2024-07 with 54 articles. The tone is markedly more negative than ordinary news coverage, at 1.57 negative stories per positive against 0.58 for all news. It is driven by heavy rainfall, torrential rain and flash floods, set against concerns over drainage, governance and infrastructure. 618 stories fall in the top priority bands, which is not a measure of tone.

text.themes_time: Between 2021 and 2025 the themed coverage of urban flooding shifted from weather and disaster stories towards government, politics and infrastructure. Environment stayed close to level, at 22.3% in 2021 and 22.2% in 2025. Weather fell from 23.3% to 15.5%, disaster from 13.5% to 10.7% and local news from 12.6% to 8.8%. Government rose from 5.4% to 9.6%, politics from 5.9% to 8.2% and infrastructure from 3.2% to 5.8%, while technology went from 1.6% to 3.2%, sustainability from 0.5% to 1.8%, and science from 5.4% to 5.3%.
text.aud0: Research output on the topic has grown, from 47 papers in 2017 to 183 in 2025, with 184 in 2024, within an index of 105,414 research papers. The no-change scenario holds the central figure at 183 for 2026 to 2028, with a sensitivity range that widens from 126 to 240 in 2026 and 12 to 354 in 2028. Exposure is large and concentrated: 1.81 billion people are directly exposed to 1-in-100-year floods, 1.24 billion of them in South and East Asia, and 89% of the world's flood-exposed people live in low- and middle-income countries. Recent news items point to Assam, Uttarakhand-area flood works (Rangirkhal) and municipalities in Edomex, though only 8 news articles are indexed, so this is thin. Policy and government themes have grown in share of coverage, which fits a shift towards institutional questions. At city scale, one study found 83.72% of documented waterlogging points in predicted high-hazard zones, and 6.41% of the central urban area was extreme-hazard.

text.aud1: For the claim that impervious surfaces increase urban flooding, the paper corpus is strongly positive: of 47 papers, 30 support, 7 qualify, none contradict and 10 are neutral, with 14.9% contested. However, no verified document verdict supports or contradicts the claim; the read documents were tallied as 7 unrelated and 1 unread, so no wording recommendation is made. The top sources are reviews and articles on impervious surface mapping and water quality, led by a 2002 review with 683 citations, and they are not direct flood-outcome tests. Head to head, green infrastructure reducing urban flooding (1,202 papers, 28.6% contested) has more evidence behind it than drainage capacity upgrades (5,802 papers, 27.9% contested). In the green infrastructure case, 3 read documents support it, while none of the 11 read for drainage upgrades did. Rainfall intensity is the only screening row with a figure: up to 18% increase in extreme precipitation, from a study in China.

New work covers flood exposure and poverty in 188 countries, flood estimation in the Cauvery River, India, and a hazard framework for Rizhao, China. text.triangulation: The claim that impervious surfaces increase urban flooding looks well supported at corpus level but is not verified at document level. Of 47 papers in the corpus, 30 are supporting, 7 qualifying, 0 contradicting and 10 neutral, with contested_pct of 14.9. The tool itself warns that such positive framing can mean consensus or publication bias. The documents actually read tell a weaker story: 9 were judged unrelated and 1 unread, and the counter-evidence search found 0 supporting, 0 contradicting, 0 qualifying, 7 unrelated and 1 unread. The tool therefore states that no verified document verdict supports a wording recommendation. The top sources are reviews and articles on water quality, remote sensing mapping and stream temperature, not flood outcomes, which is consistent with the unrelated verdicts. A careful researcher would read the sources that link imperviousness to flood peaks or runoff directly, and would not treat the absence of contradiction as confirmation.
text.head_to_head: On the measures given, green infrastructure has more evidence behind it than drainage capacity upgrades, according to the tool's verdict, although the picture is thin. Green infrastructure has 1,202 papers on both poles against 5,802 for drainage upgrades, so the larger literature belongs to drainage. The verdict rests on documents read: 3 supports for green infrastructure and 0 for drainage, where all 11 read were unrelated and 1 unread. Contested shares are close, at 28.6 for green infrastructure and 27.9 for drainage. The strongest source for each was itself judged unrelated (a 2009 article on green roofs; a 2015 review on urbanisation and water management), so neither headline source directly backs its claim. This comparison does not show that either intervention works better or cheaper in practice. A careful researcher would look at the 3 supporting green infrastructure documents and find drainage studies that report measured flood outcomes.
text.screening: Screening asked how six factors affect urban flood risk and found a quoted figure for only one. Rainfall intensity returned 'up to 18%' as an increase in extreme precipitation, from 3 papers, with the source being a 2016 study of summer rainfall in China. That is a measure of rainfall change, not of flood damage or flood risk, and no population was reported. Impervious surfaces, drainage capacity, wetland loss, urbanisation and climate change returned no value. Urbanisation returned no source at all. Several of the sources listed are off-topic, for example waterbird migration for wetland loss and residential water demand for climate change, which suggests retrieval mismatch rather than evidence. The absence of figures means the screen could not find them, not that the effects are small or absent. A careful researcher would query these factors with more specific wording and check the one figure against its original sentence.
text.framing: Framing across 2017 to 2025 is steady rather than drifting. Positive share ranges from 20.0 in 2019 to 26.5 in both 2018 and 2023, and sits at 25.2 in 2025. Contested share ranges from 13.6 in 2023 to 17.1 in 2021, ending at 15.6 in 2025. No clear direction emerges: the lowest positive year and the highest contested year are different years, and both measures move up and down. The data say how papers frame their own findings, not whether the findings are right. A careful researcher would read this as no evidence of a shift toward hope or caution and would look at sub-topics before drawing conclusions.
text.frontier: The newest work listed is varied and mostly adjacent to the core question. It includes a 2022 Nature Communications paper on flood exposure and poverty in 188 countries, a 2024 comparison of flood estimation models in the Cauvery River, a 2025 landslide mapping study of India, a 2025 flood hazard framework for Rizhao, China, and a 2025 kriging paper on urban microclimate. None has citation counts or orientation labels, so none can be ranked by influence. The framing shift compares 57,756 recent papers (22.8 cautionary_pct) with 47,658 earlier ones (26.9), a delta of -4.1 percentage points, which the tool reads as broadly unchanged. The caveat is that orientation labels a paper's own framing, not the truth. The frontier list shows interest in exposure, poverty and hazard mapping, but it does not show which topics are under-covered, since no coverage gaps were returned. A careful researcher would check the poverty and exposure work for relevance to urban drainage.
text.gaps: All three components of the claim were found to have a literature: impervious surfaces increase stormwater runoff, stormwater runoff increases urban flooding, and impervious surfaces raise flood risk. Each is marked 'yes'. This indicates there are no obvious missing links in the causal chain. It does not show how strong, how recent or how directly relevant that literature is. The triangulation result is a caution here, since the documents read were judged unrelated and no verified verdict was reached. A 'yes' means papers exist, not that they support the component. A careful researcher would sample the literature for each link and test whether the evidence is quantitative, local or only conceptual.
text.history: Title-matched papers rose from 47 in 2017 to 184 in 2024 and 183 in 2025, with a dip to 69 in 2020. Growth was gradual through 2022 at 87, then jumped to 127 in 2023 and 184 in 2024. The chosen scenario baseline is no_change, so the central value is 183 for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028. The sensitivity band widens from 126 to 240 in 2026, 69 to 297 in 2027 and 12 to 354 in 2028. The flat central line reflects the method chosen by backtesting, not a prediction that growth has stopped. Counts are matched on titles, so they miss papers that cover the topic without the title wording. A careful researcher would treat 2027 and 2028 as very uncertain and wait for 2026 counts.
text.geography: Geographic triangulation returned almost nothing: Italy with a count of 1 for where it is studied, and no countries for where it is reported. This absence means the lanes could not resolve location for the claim, not that the topic is limited to Italy or that there is no coverage elsewhere. One study is too few for any pattern. Other results in this set, such as work on China, India and Congo, show that research exists in many places, but that is not part of this lane. A careful researcher would not draw regional conclusions from this output and would rely on country metadata from the papers themselves.
text.facets: The literature is mostly promising in orientation: 1,138 papers (41.6 share_pct), followed by problem_identifying at 538 (19.7), descriptive at 477 (17.4), cautionary at 252 (9.2), breakthrough at 162 (5.9), comparative at 150 (5.5) and critical at 17 (0.6). By contribution, empirical papers number 1,520, methodological 845, review 269, position 93 and theoretical 7. The leading topics are Urban Stormwater Management Solutions at 1,721 and Flood Risk Assessment and Management at 1,226, with heat island mitigation at 560. The mix suggests a solutions-focused, applied field with little critical work, but promising framing is how authors present their work, not proof of effectiveness. The most cited since 2020 are all 2025 papers with 1 or 0 citations, so they are too recent to show influence. A careful researcher would read the cautionary and critical papers for limits on solutions and treat the topic list as including adjacent subjects such as heat and wastewater.
text.workflow: Begin with triangulation to confirm the consensus around the claim and identify supporting versus qualifying evidence. Use gap mapping to verify that each component of the claim is covered, then apply screening to extract quantitative effect sizes for the risk factors. Compare alternative interventions with head‑to‑head analysis, and contextualise the narrative with framing and frontier scans to detect shifts in optimism or emerging work. Finally, assess the growth trajectory via history, locate geographic gaps, and employ faceted browsing to focus on the most relevant empirical and methodological literature.
